messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Makoa, a 48‑year‑old roofer from the Pacific Northwest, has lived in a cycle of vigilance that began on a rainy afternoon in 2014 when a young man he had known since childhood was forced into a dark, cramped parking lot to a man who assaulted him. The assailant had struck him repeatedly, using a blunt object and a knife, then fled. The trauma left Makoa with a scar on his forearm that he keeps hidden under long sleeves, but it was the memory of the assault that has haunted him ever since. When the news first broke about a similar assault in his own town, the words on the television screen seemed to echo the violence he had endured. The very sight of headlines that echoed the words “rape” and “violence” pulled him out of the present, into the instant he had been bound. The sound of a motorcycle engine, the smell of burnt rubber on a Saturday night, and the familiar scent of beer in the bar on a Friday—all these sensory cues became triggers that pulled him back into the assault, often without any clear image in his mind. The visceral reaction was immediate: his heart raced, sweat poured down his back, and a sense of helplessness that had haunted him since the attack surged through him. This connection between triggers and the intense memory of the assault forced Makoa to keep himself away from almost any situation that could provoke a similar physical response. He no longer accepted calls from his sister to hang out on a Sunday, knowing that a sudden burst of traffic noise could bring the memory of that night to life. Because the event feels more real than any ordinary recollection, the memory itself seems to amplify every trigger. Whenever he hears a news report about sexual assault, the vividness of the assault spikes in his mind, making him hyper‑aware of the surrounding environment. The memory, in turn, heightens his anxiety over seemingly mundane stimuli, like the clanging of metal on a construction site. As the memory looms larger, Makoa finds himself avoiding situations that would place his body under physical stress; he does not engage in hard labor or strenuous activity that might remind him of the violence he once experienced. In practice, this avoidance has taken the form of steering clear of any job that involves climbing ladders or using heavy equipment. The more he avoids these stimuli, the stronger his memories of the assault become, creating a loop that tightens with each passing day. To keep his body in a state of “controlled calm,” Makoa has adopted a regimen of restricted eating. He measures portions carefully, ensuring he never feels the sensation of fullness that might trigger discomfort. The act of counting calories, he believes, gives him a sense of mastery that he no longer feels in his body after the assault. This strict eating pattern has become a cornerstone of his coping, a way of reasserting control over a life that feels precarious. At the same time, he has made himself perpetually busy. He spends long hours on his roof, clinging to the rhythm of hammering nails and measuring shingle length, believing that keeping his mind occupied will prevent him from dwelling on the past. These two maladaptive strategies—restricting physical stress and staying busy—were adopted after each trigger episode, each time the memory of the assault erupted in his mind. They are Makoa’s way of preventing the mind from sliding back into that night, even though they only reinforce the memory’s hold over him. The memory also feeds back into his avoidance. Each time he hears the clatter of a motorcycle or a bar’s laughter, the image of the assault is not a clear picture but an emotional tide that washes over him. He feels an overwhelming grief that feels like a weight on his chest, a sorrow that is not directed at anyone but at the violence that still lingers. That grief intensifies his need to stay busy; the more he fills his schedule, the less time he has to sit with those heavy emotions. He believes that by constantly being productive, he can drown out the grief that keeps him from working and from enjoying time with his wife. Yet each day he feels that the grief grows, feeding his memory’s vividness and the cycle of avoidance. Makoa’s work has suffered. The very jobs that once gave him pride now feel threatening, as each physical task could trigger a flashback. He has begun to miss deadlines, and his boss has raised concerns about his safety on the roof. At home, the conversation with his wife has become strained; she worries about his well‑being and the growing distance between them. The last week, after a particularly intense flashback triggered by a news report about a sexual assault in the local newspaper, Makoa found himself unable to sleep. He sat on the edge of his bed, breathing heavily, and realized that the cycle had reached a tipping point. He could no longer tolerate the constant fear of a trigger bringing him back to that night. It was the cumulative toll of these episodes—of the persistent avoidance, the constant busying of his mind, the unending grief, and the strain on his marriage—that finally pushed Makoa to seek help. He is most afraid that he will never escape the memory’s grip and that his life will be forever shaped by that night. Yet he also holds a fragile hope that, through understanding and support, he might learn to let the memories be a part of him rather than the definition of him.
